column3: It is the closest parallel, joining God's reality, the nullity of what is invoked besides Him, and His supreme greatness.
The preceding local ayah grounds divine supremacy in governance of the alternating night and day.
Its contrast between arrogant self-exaltation and the truly exalted offers a limited angle on divine highness.
It directly identifies God as the Truth and makes that claim concrete through His power over life and death.
The nearby rain-and-revival scene supplies a further local instance of effective divine governance.
It sharply contrasts following falsehood with following truth from God.
It pairs God's judgment in truth with the incapacity of those invoked besides Him to decide anything.
God's possession of all things and self-sufficiency support the focus's claim of unmatched greatness.
Iblis's arrogance is only an indirect contrast to the greatness that belongs to God.
God's complete knowledge of what people invoke besides Him supports the focus's critique of rival calls.
Its local catalogue of divine control over earth, sea, and sky adds a secondary illustration of effective rule.
It directly sets the arrival of truth against falsehood's inability to initiate or restore anything.
It closely joins exclusive invocation of God, divine judgment, and the names the Most High and Great.
The local sequence of life, death, and renewed life gives only broad support for divine power.
It identifies truth as coming from the Lord and frames belief and disbelief as consequential responses.
Its declaration that truth comes and falsehood perishes is a concise counterpart to the focus's central contrast.
The call to a grave event does not materially clarify truth, false worship, or divine greatness.
It contrasts the responsive call to God with futile appeals to others.
Its repudiation of fabricated partners develops the focus's rejection of rivals to God.
God's protective authority over believers and the lack of such protection for disbelievers add a related consequence.
It explicitly declares God far exalted above what people associate with Him.
It frames divine action as establishing truth and nullifying falsehood, though in a different setting.
Its language of calling back those who turned away provides only a distant resonance with invocation.
It portrays worship directed to false objects and a rebellious power, supporting the focus's warning about rival invocation.
The ordered interchange of night and day offers another, now redundant, sign of divine governance.
Its limits on intercession reinforce that all effective authority remains subject to God's permission.
The command to glorify the Most High Lord supports exaltation but adds little beyond the focus's own epithet.
Its principle concerning changed favors does not clarify the focus's truth-falsehood contrast.
The superiority of creation over human creation contributes an argument from divine magnitude.
God's ownership of all in the heavens and earth, and His high greatness, directly supports the final clause.
Its exhortation and assurance of God's presence have only limited relevance to the focus.
The description of God as knower of the unseen and the Great, Most Exalted strongly illuminates divine transcendence.
Noah's persistent call concerns human proclamation rather than the validity of what is invoked.
Its contrast of outcomes for wrongdoers and believers is not specifically tied to the focus's claims.
It presents final divine judgment but does not directly address truth, false gods, or exaltation.
The Throne Verse's designation of God as the Most High, Great is a strong lexical-theological counterpart, though it repeats a claim already well covered.
The differing attitudes toward the Hour do not substantially develop the focus.
It states that the true account includes that there is no deity except God.
The elevated register of the righteous has only a remote connection to God's own highness.
God's payment in full and disclosure of the manifest truth connect truth with final accountability.
Its proclamation of God's transcendence over association is relevant but less focused than the direct parallels.
The nearby ayah directly exposes an object invoked besides God as unable to bring harm or benefit.
It places authority with the true God and links Him to the best reward and outcome.
The Book's coming with truth gives a general revelatory parallel without treating rival invocation.
The good news to believers adds no distinct understanding of the focus.
God as Provider and possessor of strength offers a complementary account of effective divine power.
Its summons to faith and reference to covenant are only broadly related to acknowledging God.
Its warning about worshiping others and loss is relevant but less explanatory than the direct critiques of false gods.
The alliances and social consequences of disbelief do not clarify the focus's theological contrast.
It denies independent intercession to those invoked besides God, except within God's own truth and knowledge.
The mission to Pharaoh's leaders has no material connection to the focus.
It explicitly joins God's removal of falsehood with His establishment of truth by His words.
Its denial that creation is aimless supports an ordered reality, but only indirectly supports the focus's truth claim.
It questions turning to what cannot benefit or harm apart from God, closely reinforcing the futility of rival calls.
The fulfillment of judgment against disbelievers offers only a distant consequence of rejection.
God's absolute oneness is foundational support for denying any valid rival invocation.
Its prohibition on mixing or concealing truth with falsehood gives a direct ethical-revelatory form of the focus's contrast.
It directly challenges those who take protectors besides God and invoke them as intermediaries.
God's dominion over heaven and earth and the loss of falsifiers on the Hour combine two supporting themes.
It states the incapacity of those invoked besides God to create, directly explaining their nullity.
The highest horizon is not a statement about God's own exaltation or exclusive divinity.
It explicitly names God the true King and commands recognition of His transcendence.
It depicts truth prevailing and false works becoming void, a vivid counterpart to the focus's contrast.
It joins God's transcendent true kingship with the denial of any deity besides Him.
The command to call for repeated destruction does not clarify which invocation is true or false.
The divisions among inheritors of the Book do not materially develop the focus.
Its portrait of arrogant refusal of revelation indirectly contrasts human pride with divine greatness.
It forbids associating with God without authority, directly supporting the rejection of illegitimate rivals.
Calling to good concerns communal ethics rather than calling upon God or others.
The nearby portrait of unstable worship of God reveals a related failure to hold to true devotion.
It depicts former objects of invocation as absent and useless at judgment.
It calls supposed deities mere names without divine authority and reserves judgment and worship for God alone.
It assigns all grandeur in the heavens and earth to God, directly reinforcing His greatness.
The emphatic divine declaration of truth supports truth as the basis of decisive judgment.
It identifies truth as from the Lord but adds little after the stronger truth declarations.
Its parable distinguishes passing froth from what benefits and remains, vividly developing truth's endurance over falsehood.
The escalating signs given to Pharaoh's people do not clarify the focus's core claims.
Its reference to acting without right is a distant use of the truth-falsehood field.
Noah's public call is about prophetic persistence, not the validity of objects of invocation.
The true divine promise reinforces God's reliability but does not address false worship or exaltation directly.
God's hearing of prayer gives only a narrow, indirect support for directing invocation to Him.
It forbids worshiping those invoked besides God and links such worship to deviation from guidance.
God's good pleasure being greater than the gardens offers a meaningful, though indirect, measure of divine greatness.
Its institutional signs and comprehensive knowledge do not materially develop the focus.
Its question whether the objects invoked can hear directly tests the efficacy of rival invocation.
It identifies objects worshiped besides God as unable to harm or benefit and rejects their claimed intercession.
Its ban on consuming wealth through falsehood uses a different practical sense of falsehood.
God's all-encompassing knowledge broadly supports His supremacy but adds little to this focus.
It presents a truth from the Lord supported by testimony and calls for freedom from doubt.
It ends with judgment in truth and the loss of those committed to falsehood.
The statement about one of the great matters does not identify divine greatness or rival worship.
The servant's invocation of God is relevant but does not contrast it with invalid invocation.
Taking one's desire as a god is a pointed internal form of the false divinity the focus rejects.
Its rejection of truth as magic shows resistance to truth but adds little about God's exclusive reality.
Its account of corrupt listeners and distortion does not materially clarify the focus.
Its assurance that truth has come from the Lord is relevant but redundant within the reviewed set.
Devotional completion for God supports exclusive orientation but offers no direct treatment of the focus's contrast.
Reciting a narrative in truth gives a general account of truthful revelation.
The threatened summons of enforcers does not clarify divine truth, false worship, or exaltation.
The association of bringing truth with truthful speech offers a final, general reinforcement of the truth claim.
God's oneness supplies the foundational denial that any rival invocation could be valid.
The divine testimony to His exclusive deity and sustaining justice directly joins truth with uncompromised divinity.
It names association with God as a grave departure, clarifying the theological stakes of invoking others.
It gives the grave outcome of associating partners with God, extending the focus's rejection of false worship.
It tests whether anyone besides God can be called in distress, directly probing exclusive invocation.
It challenges alleged partners to answer those who call them, exposing their inability to respond.
It forbids invoking besides God what neither benefits nor harms, nearly restating the focus's criterion of futility.
God's universal creative lordship and irresistible power explain why no supposed equal can rival Him.
Its prohibition of taking two gods and declaration of one God directly supports exclusive divinity.
It contrasts worship directed besides God with the utter lack of independent provision or power in its objects.
It instructs people to call the beings they claim besides God and declares their inability to remove or alter harm.
It denies God any partner in dominion and affirms His incomparable greatness.
It condemns taking gods besides God without clear authority, directly challenging invented divinity.
It exposes the taking of gods besides God for supposed honor, contrasting imagined support with divine supremacy.
It identifies God as the sole deity whose knowledge encompasses all things.
It argues that multiple gods would corrupt heaven and earth, making cosmic order evidence for divine oneness.
It challenges the taking of other gods by demanding proof, directly contesting their claim to reality.
It questions worship of what cannot benefit or harm, a direct test of the focus's false objects.
The local passage rejects worship of that for which God sent down no authority or knowledge.
Its fly parable vividly demonstrates that those invoked besides God lack even the smallest creative power.
It rejects both divine offspring and any other deity, grounding God's uniqueness in the coherence of creation.
It affirms God's sole dominion and denies Him any partner in creation or rule.
It describes supposed gods besides Him as unable to create, harm, benefit, or control life and death.
Abraham's questions about whether objects of worship benefit or harm directly test their alleged divinity.
The repeated question whether any god is with God uses creation and provision to deny partners.
It contrasts God's response to the distressed with the claim that another god could share His authority.
It identifies worship of idols with fabrication and returns provision and worship to God alone.
It names associating partners with God as a great wrong, marking the opposite of the focus's exclusive claim.
It calls on alleged partners besides God to show any share in heaven or earth, exposing their lack of power.
It asks whether any creator besides God provides from heaven and earth, directly connecting creation to exclusive deity.
It depicts taking gods besides God in hope of help, setting up the failure of that expectation.
Its concise declaration that the deity is one provides an unambiguous counterpart to the focus's monotheism.
It invokes God's acknowledged creation of heaven and earth to undermine reliance on rivals.
It rejects being commanded to worship others besides God, making exclusive worship explicit.
It names God as creator of all things and declares that no deity exists except Him.
It commands invocation and devotion to the Ever-Living God alone, who has no deity besides Him.
It rebukes making equals with the Lord of the worlds, directly opposing association.
It records acknowledgement of God as Creator, providing a basis for exposing inconsistent rival worship.
It challenges those who call on others besides God to show what their objects created or own.
It commands that no other deity be set alongside God, an explicit formulation of the focus's exclusive claim.
Its rhetorical denial of any deity besides God directly reinforces divine oneness and transcendence.
It begins the concentrated divine-name passage by declaring that there is no deity except God.
It pairs God's exclusive deity with the names that establish His sovereign transcendence and greatness.
It declares that no deity exists except God and directs believers to place reliance in Him alone.
It states that the Messenger calls only upon his Lord and associates none with Him.
It names God as Lord of east and west, declares no deity but Him, and directs reliance exclusively to Him.
